2.1 Applying technology to 
collect data

Sensors 
Sensors, such as digital thermometers and pH probes, are used to measure 
physical properties and transmit the results to other devices for processing. 
Maodern digital sensors are more compact, accurate and precise than 
traditional analogue devices. In addition, digital sensors can be connected to 
data loggers that collect and save measurement results at regular intervals. 
Like any scientific instruments, sensors require regular checks and calibration. 
This is particularly important forsensors that measure a certain property 
continuously, as any malfunction or loss of accuracy in this type of equipment can 
remain unnoticed for a long time and invalidate important experimental results. 
In a school laboratory, students can use their smartphones as sensors for various 
experiments, which include analytical chemistry, kinetics and microscopy. 
A suitable app can turn a smartphone into a portable colorimeter or digital 
thermometer. Videc recordings or series of photographs can be used for detailed 
examination of very fast or very slow changes in colour, turbidity or aggregate 
state (e.g. crystal growth) that are difficult to observe in real time. A smartphone 
with a camera can recognize names or CAS numbers of chemicals and display 
various information on their properties, hazards, handling and disposal. 
Databases 
Databases store large amounts of structured information that is easy to search, 
analyse, retrieve and update. Most chemistry-related databases contain 
information on a particular topic, for example: 
» chemical elements (e.g., WebElements, University of Sheffield, UK) 
* physical properties of substances (e.g., Chemspider, Royal Society of 
Chemistry, UK) 
* thermodynamics (e.g., NIST Chemistry WebBook, National Institute of 
Standards and Technology, USA) 
* spectroscopic data (e.g. SDBSWeb, National Institute of Advanced 
Industrial Science and Technology, Japan). 
In most cases, researchers use databases to obtain information on one or 
just a few chemical compounds, but some databases offer advanced tools 
for processing large numbers of entries in order to discover trends and 
correlations between various properties of the studied compounds.

The data in a spreadsheet can be plotted as a graph or presented as a 
diagram. For example, the calibration curve in figure 25 was created in Excel. 
The plots of scattered or uncertain data can be enhanced by adding a best-fit 
line or curve, intercepts and error bars (see Tool 3.4).

2.2 Applying technology to process data 
Models 
Models are simplifications of complex systems that allow us to focus on a 
particular property or feature of the studied compound, process or concept. 
For example, a ball-and-stick model (see figure 26) shows the three￾dimensional arrangement of atoms and bond angles in an individual molecule 
while the ideal gas model (Structure 1.5) predicts the collective behaviour of 
molecules in gaseous state. 
The relationship between two variables can be modelled using a spreadsheet. 
For example, a set of experimental data, such as concentrations of standard 
solutions and their absorbances at a specific wavelength, can be used to build 
a calibration curve using a best-fit line (see figure 25). The resulting graph 
can then be used to extend the set of data by interpolation or extrapolation 
(Tool 3.4) and thus determine the unknown concentration of ananalyte in 
solution with a known absorbance. 
More complex spreadsheet models allow us to investigate thermodynamics, 
kinetics or equilibria in various systems involving more than two variables. 
Spreadsheet modelling can be used as a part of your research project for 
internal assessment.

Practice problems for T2 
Problem 1 
In a chemical experiment, the electrical conductivity and pH of the 
studied solution must be recorded simultaneously every second for a 
period of 1 minute. Suggest the type(s) of equipment that can be used in 
this experiment. 
Problem 2 
US chemists T. Kuntzleman and E. Jacobson devised a way to use 
a smartphone with an RGB app as a colorimeter. Their paper was 
published in the Journal of Chemical Education, 2016, vol. 93, pp. 1249- 
1252, DOI10.1021/acs.jchemed.5b00844. Find and read the abstract 
of this paper (or the whole paper if your school has access to it) and 
outline the advantages and disadvantages of the approach used by the 
authors. 
Problem 3 
Using a database of your choice, explore melting points, boiling points 
and densities of group 1 elements. 
Problem 4 
Using a spreadsheet, list the values of the element properties from 
problem 3 and draw graphs of these properties against the period 
numbers of these elements. 
Problem 5 
Describe the operation performed by each of the following spreadsheet 
formulas. 
a) =(8.31*A1)/(B2*B3) 
b) =SUM(B1:B10) 
c) =AVERAGE(B2,B3,B5) 
Problem 6
Outline how you would construct a spreadsheet-based model to 
illustrate the following concepts. 
a) The relationship between the concentration of sulfuric acid, 
H,S0,(aqg) and the pH of its solution. 
b) The correlation between melting and boiling points of group 
1 elements. 
c) Le Chatelier’s principle for the system 2NH (g) = N,(g) + 3H,(g).

A digital pH probe and a digital conductivity probe connected to a data logger or computer. Alternatively, any pH and conductivity probes (digital or analogue) can be used if their readings are recorded continuously using a video camera or a mobile phone.
Advantages: simple protocol, no specialized laboratory equipment or materials are required, data are recorded automatically, video recordings of experiments can be reviewed later.
Disadvantages: low accuracy and low precision, the results are affected by external lighting, calibration is problematic.
In addition to the database of your choice, the melting points and boiling points (but not density) of group 1 elements are listed in section 8 of the data booklet.
Your plots should be similar to figure 9 in Student Book Structure 3.2.
The value 8.31 (probably the gas constant, R) is multiplied by the value in cell A1 and divided by the product of values in cells B2 and B3.
The sum of the values in cells B1 through B10 is calculated.
The average (mean) of the values in cells B2, B3 and B5 is calculated.
Each model can be constructed in many ways. One example is given for each model using standard Microsoft Excel functions.
The concentration of sulfuric acid (in mol dm−3) is entered as a numerical value in cell A1, and the solution pH is calculated automatically in any other cell using the following formula:
=-log(A1*2)
Notice that each mole of H2SO4(aq) produces two H+(aq) ions, hence the coefficient “2” in the formula.
If more than one pair of concentration and pH values must be shown simultaneously, the list of concentrations can be entered in column A, and the formula can be copied to all cells in column B (the cell references will be updated automatically).
In examination papers, you will not be expected to provide Excel expressions. To score full marks, you will only need to mention that the concentration is entered in one cell and the pH is calculated using a reference to that cell and a spreadsheet-specific mathematical expression.
The melting points (in °C or K) are entered in column A, the boiling points (in the same units) are entered in column B, and a scatter plot is constructed using the data in these two columns. The best-fit line (trendline) or best-fit curve is drawn using the internal functionality of the spreadsheet software. The R2 value and the equation of the best-fit line or curve are calculated by the software and shown on the plot.
The concentrations (in mol dm−3) of NH3(g), N2(g) and H2(g) are entered in cells A1, A2 and A3, respectively. The value of the equilibrium constant (K) at a given temperature is entered in cell A4. The reaction quotient (Q) is calculated automatically in cell A5 using the following formula:
=A2*A3^3/A1^2
The values of K and Q can be compared either visually or using Boolean operators. For example, the following expression will display the direction of favoured reaction (forward, reverse or neither):
=IF(A5<A4,"forward",IF(A5>A4,"reverse","neither"))
This model can be used to predict the effects of concentrations of NH3(g), N2(g) and H2(g) on the equilibrium position. Similar approaches can be used for modelling the effects of pressure and temperature.
